content: The best available diagnostic tests should be utilized to ensure optimal outcomes at both individual and public health levels. All laboratory tests conducted and the reports generated for patient management must adhere to the highest quality standards. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a tool to assist laboratories in implementing a quality management system. Laboratories should seek accreditation from a recognized national or international body, such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), to maintain high-quality services. The goal is to achieve compliance with the international standard ISO 15189. Accreditation involves an external audit to confirm the laboratory's ability to provide high-quality services, based on a defined standard of practice verified through peer review. While this process does not assess the appropriateness of molecular tests chosen for diagnosing sexually transmitted infections (STIs), laboratories are expected to provide evidence of the performance capabilities of these tests before incorporating them into STI services. Laboratories meeting these criteria are considered to have quality-assured molecular testing with a fully operational management system. For STI prevention and control, WHO recommends that laboratories aim to minimize the time between sample collection and the delivery of results to patients, ideally providing results on the same day as the visit. Laboratories should also establish quality indicators with targets for rapid turnaround times. Prompt and effective treatment of STIs, ideally administered on the same day as the patient’s first contact with a healthcare provider, is a critical public health measure to interrupt the transmission chain of infections without delay. Countries should adopt national standardized treatment protocols for STIs to ensure that all patients receive appropriate and adequate treatment across all levels of healthcare services. These protocols also facilitate the training and supervision of healthcare providers and help reduce the risk of antimicrobial resistance development. A standardized list of antimicrobial agents can further streamline the procurement of medicines. The recommendations in this document are intended to help countries develop standardized flow charts tailored to local epidemiological conditions and antimicrobial susceptibility data. National guidelines for effective STI management should be developed in close collaboration with local STI and public health experts, as well as laboratory professionals. A flow chart is a diagrammatic representation that guides healthcare providers through a series of actions and decisions to address a clinical problem. Flow charts typically include an entry point (the presenting symptom), decision points (yes/no questions), and action boxes (treatment, counseling, health education, or referral). Standard symbols, such as rectangles for actions and diamonds for decisions, are often used to ensure clarity and consistency. ISO 5807 specifies the standard flow chart symbols for information processing. To use a flow chart, one starts at the clinical problem box and follows the steps until reaching an exit box, which represents the resolution of the issue. The syndromic approach to managing STIs, such as urethral discharge syndrome, involves identifying and treating infections based on symptoms and clinical findings. Urethral discharge in men is commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, or other pathogens like Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis. The prevalence of these pathogens varies geographically and by population group. Countries should periodically conduct studies to identify the most prevalent and significant causes of urethral discharge in their settings. Men with urethritis typically present with urethral discharge, with or without dysuria (painful urination). Dysuria or itching at the urethral opening may sometimes be the only symptoms. On examination, urethral discharge may range from scanty to copious and from clear to purulent. However, distinguishing between gonorrhea, chlamydia, or other causes of urethritis based on clinical presentation alone is not possible. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the gold standard for detecting C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in men and women, including pharyngeal and anorectal samples. For anorectal samples in men who have sex with men, testing for C. trachomatis genovars associated with lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is recommended to guide appropriate treatment. First-catch urine or urethral swabs are suitable specimens for NAAT. For M. genitalium, NAAT is the most effective detection method, although testing is not yet widely available. For T. vaginalis, NAAT offers the highest sensitivity among diagnostic methods. Residual genital swab samples used for diagnosing chlamydia and gonorrhea via NAAT are also effective for detecting T. vaginalis nucleic acids. Culture methods remain the standard for antimicrobial susceptibility testing of N. gonorrhoeae, but the organism is challenging to grow in the laboratory, requiring specialized training and media. As a result, culture is not routinely performed in resource-limited settings. Similarly, culture methods for T. vaginalis are no longer widely used due to the advent of point-of-care antigen tests and NAAT. Microscopy can identify N. gonorrhoeae through Gram-stained samples, with a presumptive diagnosis made if Gram-negative diplococci are observed intracellularly in polymorphonuclear leukocytes. However, microscopy does not allow differentiation of Gram-negative cocci. For urethral discharge, a negative Gram stain for intracellular diplococci may suggest non-gonococcal urethritis. Management of urethral discharge should be based on quality-assured molecular assays. WHO recommends performing molecular assays, such as NAAT, to confirm or exclude N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Treatment should be administered based on test results on the same day. If urethral discharge is present but tests are negative, treatment for non-gonococcal and non-chlamydial urethritis (e.g., M. genitalium or T. vaginalis) is recommended. In settings where same-day molecular testing is not feasible, syndromic treatment for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be initiated, with test results used to guide partner management when available. For recurrent or persistent urethral discharge, repeat molecular assays should be performed after 21 days to test for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, and T. vaginalis, as well as antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.
